content: Dental restoration, also known as dental filling, involves the use of restorative materials to artificially restore the function, integrity, and morphology of missing tooth structure. This structural loss typically occurs due to dental caries or external trauma. In some cases, tooth structure is intentionally removed during preparation to enhance the aesthetics or physical integrity of the restorative material. Dental restoration also encompasses the replacement of missing tooth structure using dental implants. Restorative materials can be classified into two main categories: direct and indirect restorations. Direct restorations are placed directly into the tooth, while indirect restorations are fabricated outside the mouth, often in a dental laboratory. Common direct restorative materials include dental amalgam, glass ionomer cement, and composite resins. Indirect restorations are typically made from materials such as acrylic, porcelain, zirconia, gold, and other metals. Tooth preparation involves removing infected or decayed tooth material to clean and shape the cavity for filling. This is usually performed using a dental drill. If a permanent restoration cannot be completed immediately, a temporary restoration is placed to protect the tooth. Direct restorations are applied directly to the tooth in situ. Materials such as amalgam (silver-colored) or dental composite (tooth-colored) are commonly used. When composite is used, it is cured with a UV light and may be polished for a smooth finish. Patients are advised to avoid chewing hard foods for a day or two after the procedure to prevent dislodging the filling. Indirect restorations include inlays, onlays, crowns, bridges, and veneers. These are fabricated by a dental technician based on records provided by the dentist. Once the fit and bite are confirmed, the restoration is permanently bonded to the tooth. While waiting for the indirect restoration to be completed, a temporary restoration may be used to maintain occlusal space, contact points, and protect the pulp tissue. Removable dental prostheses, such as dentures, are sometimes considered a form of indirect restoration. Precision attachments, including magnets, clips, hooks, and implants, can aid in securing removable prosthetics to teeth. Dental implants are increasingly used in restorative care due to advancements in technology and research. These implants, typically made of titanium or titanium alloy, are screws anchored into the maxillary or mandibular bone. They can support crowns, bridges, or prostheses. Ideally, the bone integrates with the implant's roughened surface, a process known as osseointegration. Restorations are classified based on their size and location, as per G.V. Black's classification system. For instance, a one-surface filling is categorized as Class I under this system. Materials used in dental restorations include metals, metallic alloys, dental composites, and ceramics. Metals such as titanium, gold alloys, and silver-palladium alloys are commonly used for crowns, bridges, and dentures due to their biocompatibility and stability. Dental composites, also known as white fillings, are used for direct fillings and can also be laboratory-fabricated for crowns and inlays. While composites are tooth-colored, they are less durable than porcelain or metal restorations and are more prone to wear and discoloration. Porcelain restorations, including full-ceramic crowns and veneers, are highly desirable for their ability to mimic the color and translucency of natural enamel. Porcelain-fused-to-metal restorations combine the strength of metal with the aesthetic appeal of porcelain. Zirconium oxide, introduced through CAD/CAM technology, has revolutionized full-ceramic restorations due to its high strength and fracture toughness. It is now used for bridges, implant structures, and root dowel pins. The advent of computerized dentistry (CAD/CAM) has enabled the economical use of zirconium oxide and other advanced materials. This technology allows for the precise fabrication of restorations, such as copings and bridges, directly from digital impressions. The CEREC method is a chairside CAD/CAM restorative procedure. The dentist examines the tooth and determines the appropriate treatment, which could range from a simple filling to a full crown. An optical impression of the prepared tooth is taken using a camera, and specialized software converts this into a 3D virtual model. The restoration design is then sent to a milling machine, where a ceramic block matching the tooth shade is milled into the final restoration. Within 10-20 minutes, an all-ceramic, tooth-colored restoration is ready to be bonded in place.
